title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning with Secure Aggregation
summary: Undergraduate thesis: federated learning + secure aggregation + differential privacy, applied to wind farm SCADA telemetry. Small interactive diagrams build up to the real protocol visualiser, embedded live.

blocks.html:
Building a Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning System with Secure Aggregation

Undergraduate thesis — Bachelor of Engineering (Honours), University of Sydney, MINT Research Group. Supervised by Dr. Ali Shakiba.

Short version: wind farms don't want to share their sensor data with each other, and honestly, fair enough — it's commercially sensitive and there are regulations about it. So this thesis builds a system that trains one shared model across several wind farms' data without any of that data ever leaving home, and then goes a step further to make sure the training process itself can't be spied on either.

items: The problem: wind farm operators each hold rich turbine sensor data, but competitive and legal reasons keep it siloed — individually too small to train good models, collectively plenty.
The build: Federated Learning (train across farms, data stays put) + Secure Aggregation (the server can't even peek at individual updates) + optional Differential Privacy (a formal guarantee on top).

The finding: Secure Aggregation is free — identical accuracy to plain federated training. Differential Privacy is not — it's a real, steep, measured cost. Keeping the data siloed at all costs more than either.
Try it: three small diagrams below let you break each idea yourself, then the actual protocol visualiser built for this thesis runs all three together on the real data.

blocks.html:
Wind power is now a serious part of the global energy mix — installed capacity passed 1,347 GW at the end of 2025, meeting over 11% of world electricity demand, and it's forecast to nearly double by 2030. Keeping that fleet running is expensive: operations and maintenance account for roughly 20–25% of the levelised cost of wind energy, and better fault-detection models are a direct lever on that cost.

The obstacle is data. Every wind farm operator collects rich SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) telemetry from its turbines, but that data almost never leaves the organisation — competitive sensitivity and regulations like the GDPR make centralising it a non-starter. The result is a fragmented set of data silos, each individually too small to train a reliable predictive model, but collectively more than enough.

This thesis builds and evaluates a system that trains one shared model across those silos without the raw data ever leaving any of them, using real wind turbine SCADA data from the public CARE benchmark (three wind farms). The three ideas below each get their own small diagram first — the full protocol visualiser, where they all run together on the real data, is waiting at the end.

In ordinary machine learning you centralise the data and train one model on all of it. Federated Learning (FL) inverts that: a shared model is trained across distributed clients — here, wind farms — without any client's raw data ever leaving its own site.

Each round works the same way. The server broadcasts the current global model to the clients. Each client trains it briefly on its own local data and sends back only the resulting parameter adjustments — never the data itself. The server then combines those updates, weighted by how much data each client trained on:

wt+1 ← Σk (nk / n) · wkt+1

This is Federated Averaging (FedAvg), the workhorse of the field. A client holding ten times the data of its peers gets ten times the influence over the shared model — which matters here, because wind farms vary in fleet size by an order of magnitude. The diagram below strips everything else away: three clients, fixed data sizes, one aggregate.

blocks.caption: Click run round a few times to see each farm report a fresh local number and the weighted aggregate update. Then click a farm's box to take it offline and run another round — its weight drops out of the aggregate entirely.

blocks.label: wind farms in the CARE benchmark — the entire client population this system trains across, dozens of times smaller than FL was originally built for

blocks.html: FL was designed and proven at huge scale — Google's production deployment handles roughly 10 million daily active phones. Wind farm operators are the opposite: a handful of identifiable companies, each holding a large, high-quality dataset. This is the cross-silo regime, and it changes which problems actually matter, as the next section shows.

Federated Learning's promise — "the data never leaves the site" — turns out to be incomplete. The gradient update each client sends back still carries a lot of information about the data it was computed from. Geiping et al. showed that high-resolution training images can be reconstructed from a single gradient vector, with nothing more than a standard honest-but-curious server — one that follows the protocol correctly but inspects every message it receives. Keeping data local isn't enough if the updates themselves leak it.

Secure Aggregation (SecAgg), introduced by Bonawitz et al., closes that gap by cryptographically masking each client's update before it ever reaches the server. Each client adds a private mask and a set of pairwise masks it has agreed with every other client via Diffie–Hellman key exchange:

ŷu = wu + bu + Σv≠u su,v

The pairwise masks are constructed to cancel out exactly when everything is summed, so the server recovers the aggregate and nothing else. Below, the same three farms now mask their numbers before sending — watch what the server can and can't see.

blocks.caption: Masking is on by default — run a round and notice the server only sees a masked packet per farm, yet the total still comes out right. Turn masking off to compare. Then set τ and drop farms until fewer than τ remain — the round aborts instead of revealing anything.

blocks.label: lose one farm and you're already at the abort boundary — at K=3, dropping a single client is a third of the whole network, not a rounding error

blocks.html: That's where the wind-farm setting gets interesting. SecAgg was designed and evaluated at K in the hundreds to millions, where losing a handful of clients is noise. At K=3, this thesis's first research question is precisely whether SecAgg's guarantees and behaviour hold up gracefully at a client count this small.

SecAgg solves one problem — the server never sees any individual update — but it doesn't limit what the aggregate itself reveals about any one record. That's what Differential Privacy (DP) is for: a formal guarantee that a mechanism's output is nearly indistinguishable whether or not any single record was included in its input. That's a claim about an observer's ability to tell two adjacent datasets apart, not just about numbers wobbling — the diagram below shows exactly that.

blocks.caption: At the default low σ, release a dozen samples and notice the two clusters stay apart — you can mostly tell which dataset produced which point. Drag σ up and release more: the clusters blur together, and that loss of distinguishability is the actual privacy guarantee, not just ‘the number moved’.

blocks.html:
In practice this means adding calibrated noise. The standard recipe (DP-SGD) clips each client's update to a bounded norm C, then adds Gaussian noise before aggregation:

noise ~ N(0, σ²C²)

Larger σ means stronger privacy — and an unavoidable utility cost. SecAgg and DP are complementary, not interchangeable: SecAgg hides who sent what; DP bounds how much any one record could have moved the result.

blocks.label: mean RMSE at σ=2.0 versus no noise at all, measured on this thesis's own prototype — strong privacy is not a free lunch

blocks.caption: Measured privacy–utility trade-off: RMSE vs. DP noise multiplier σ, averaged across the three real CARE wind farms.
Measured convergence: FedAvg alone vs. FedAvg through SecAgg are identical to six decimal places — the masking recovers exactly the same aggregate, at no accuracy cost.

blocks.html:
The literature has mature theory for SecAgg and established applications of FL to industrial sensor data — but nothing that puts both together on a real regression task at the client counts a wind-energy deployment would actually have. That gap motivates two research questions:

RQ1 — How can Secure Multiparty Computation primitives, particularly Secure Aggregation, be effectively integrated into a federated learning system to provide privacy guarantees during model update aggregation?

RQ2 — To what extent do current secure aggregation protocols maintain individual client privacy when tested on real-world regression tasks using wind turbine SCADA telemetry?

A first, small-scale prototype (one real CARE event file per farm, a small MLP, 25 FedAvg rounds) gives an early read before scaling to the thesis's full empirical chapter:

blocks.note: RMSE in kW, the CARE dataset's normalised power units.

blocks.html:
Reading these numbers against the research questions: SecAgg costs nothing here — the FedAvg and FedAvg+SecAgg rows are identical to six decimal places, confirming aggregation privacy comes for free, now shown on a regression task rather than the classification benchmarks the published SecAgg evaluations use. Non-IID data costs far more than SecAgg does — FedAvg alone is 30–70% worse than pooling all the data centrally, simply the price of keeping three physically different wind sites (their ambient temperatures alone average 20°C, 12°C and 29°C) siloed at all. DP is where the real cost lives, and it's steep even at moderate noise. And small K makes dropout consequential fast: with three clients and a survival threshold of two, losing one farm for a round is already close to the abort boundary — in a 20-round dropout test, a two-farm dropout in a single round triggers an outright abort.

This is explicitly a prototype, not the thesis's final empirical result: it trains on one ~4,000-row event file per farm rather than the full 95-file / ~19GB CARE corpus, and SecAgg's arithmetic is reproduced faithfully without a real Diffie–Hellman key exchange over a network. Its purpose is to sanity-check the full pipeline before scaling up.

Everything above, in one place: the actual protocol visualiser built for this thesis, with federated rounds, dropout, Secure Aggregation and DP noise all running together on the real three-farm CARE topology — plus the measured RMSE curves available to overlay against its own live illustrative one.
